claims.text: Molecular dynamics simulations can be used to study the thermal response of FeCuCrCoNi high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
The thermal response of FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles depends on nanoparticle size.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles become thermally unstable at lower temperatures than larger ones.
Enhanced surface effects cause the proposed reduction in thermal-stability temperature for smaller nanoparticles.
The initial materials are synthesized FeCuCrCoNi high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
The nanoparticles span a range of sizes and have well-defined initial structures.
Nanoparticles of systematically varied sizes can be subjected to controlled incremental heating in MD simulations.
Nanoparticle size determines the surface-to-volume ratio.
The nanoparticle surface-to-volume ratio affects atomic diffusion.
The nanoparticle surface-to-volume ratio affects local structural rearrangements.
Smaller nanoparticles have higher surface energy and greater atomic mobility.
Higher surface energy and greater atomic mobility lower the effective activation barrier for structural transformations.
Lower effective activation barriers produce earlier thermal instability, including phase transitions or sintering.
The onset temperature for thermal instability or structural evolution decreases as nanoparticle size decreases.
Larger FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles retain bulk-like thermal stability over a higher temperature range.
The validity of the simulation results depends on whether the interatomic potential accurately represents the FeCuCrCoNi system.
Simulation timescale and potential parameterization can affect the observed thermal-transition temperatures.
Atomic diffusion coefficients and radial distribution functions can be used to monitor thermally induced structural changes.
A lack of a statistically significant decrease in instability-onset temperature for smaller particles would falsify the hypothesis.
